query: For refractory materials, experiments at the solid-to-fluid transition are difficult and yield sparse, scattered data, while the large compositional space of high-entropy systems makes systematic screening impractical. DFT free-energy studies can determine the transition from the crossing of solid and dense-fluid Gibbs energies and provide associated thermodynamic properties, but their reliance on extensive ab initio molecular dynamics makes them costly. TOR-TILD has shown high efficiency for elemental and binary systems, yet becomes substantially slower for multicomponent systems. Any broadly useful approach must retain ab initio-level accuracy, represent all thermodynamic effects identified as important, treat both phases around the transition, and remain practical across relevant compositions and temperatures. For a multicomponent high-entropy material in these high-temperature states, what single intervention could improve determination of transition temperature, fusion enthalpy and entropy, volume change, and dense-fluid heat capacity? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention and causal mechanism, its predicted outcome relative to existing experimental and computational baselines, its boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive experiment or benchmark that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Integrating a machine-learned interatomic potential (MLIP) trained on a sparse, active-learning-selected subset of DFT free-energy trajectories into the TOR-TILD framework will enable the accurate and efficient calculation of solid-to-fluid transition properties for multicomponent high-entropy materials.
generation.material_initial_state: A multicomponent high-entropy refractory material in a solid state at temperatures approaching the melting point.
generation.intervention: Replace the ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) engine in the TOR-TILD workflow with a machine-learned interatomic potential (MLIP) trained via active learning on a minimal set of high-temperature DFT snapshots, while retaining the TOR-TILD thermodynamic integration protocol.
generation.conditions: High-temperature regime near the solid-to-fluid transition (T > 0.8 T_melt) and high compositional complexity (5+ principal elements).
generation.structural_mediator: The MLIP surrogate model that captures the complex many-body interactions and anharmonic effects of the high-entropy alloy without the computational cost of DFT, allowing for the extensive sampling required by TOR-TILD.
generation.mechanism: The MLIP approximates the DFT potential energy surface with near-ab initio accuracy but at a fraction of the computational cost, enabling the generation of the dense phase-space sampling required for Gibbs free energy crossing determination in multicomponent systems where TOR-TILD with AIMD becomes prohibitively slow.
generation.predicted_outcome: The transition temperature, fusion enthalpy, entropy, volume change, and dense-fluid heat capacity will be determined with accuracy comparable to full AIMD-TOR-TILD (within 2-3%) but with a computational speedup of 2-3 orders of magnitude, making systematic screening of high-entropy systems feasible.
generation.baseline: Current state-of-the-art: Full AIMD-TOR-TILD (accurate but computationally intractable for multicomponent systems) and standard experimental methods (sparse, scattered data, difficult to perform at transition).
generation.boundary: The hypothesis holds only if the MLIP training set is sufficiently diverse to cover the configurational space of the high-entropy alloy and the specific anharmonic modes active near the transition; it may fail for systems with extreme electronic complexity or phase separation not captured by the training data.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding whether a single MLIP model can generalize across the entire compositional space of a high-entropy alloy without retraining, and whether the active learning loop can converge within a reasonable number of DFT evaluations given the high dimensionality of the configuration space.

falsification_experiment.design: Select a known multicomponent high-entropy alloy with available experimental melting data. Perform the TOR-TILD workflow using (1) full AIMD (as ground truth, limited to a small supercell/time window) and (2) the proposed MLIP-TOR-TILD workflow. Compare the predicted transition temperature and fusion enthalpy against the AIMD results and experimental values.
measurements: Solid-liquid Gibbs free energy crossing point (T_m)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the MLIP-TOR-TILD predictions deviate from the AIMD ground truth by more than 5% for T_m or ΔH_fus, or if the computational speedup is less than 10x compared to AIMD while maintaining the same accuracy.
